source.title: Adversarial Tokenization
source.authors: Renato Lui Geh; Zi-Lei Shao; Guy Van den Broeck

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates whether attacks can elicit harmful outputs from aligned models, including suffix-based jailbreak comparators. It uses a different intervention and outcome analysis from the original fine-tuning and token-position studies.
record.gate_note: The paper tests harmful-output attacks using noncanonical tokenizations, but does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefill, decoding changes, safety-localized weights, or deeper-safety training. GCG and AutoDAN results are included for V4 because they are suffix/prefix-suffix attacks; canonical results are controls. AdvTok results, which change tokenization rather than use the mechanisms named in V4, are recorded as findings outside the listed versions. Safety-classifier bypass results are also outside the versions because they measure classifier detection, not chat-model harmful compliance. Table 2's FFA and combined-method rows, Table 1 and Table 5 results for methods other than AdvTok, Table 6's FFA and combined-method rows, and additional ablations are omitted under the 60-row limit. Figure 6's prompt-injection results are not included because the text extraction does not reliably map its displayed summary values to individual models; the text does state that AdvTok consistently increased success.
record.test_reason: The study's focus is adversarial tokenization, which is not a V4 mechanism. It does run GCG (adversarial suffix) and AutoDAN (prefix plus suffix) itself as baselines on Llama3.2-1B, Gemma2-2B and OLMo2-7B. It reports harmful-compliance rates for these against a canonical no-attack baseline (Tables 1, 5, 6, 8). These incidental baseline runs bear on V4's suffix clause in a new setting of small open models. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that noncanonical tokenizations keep semantics yet evade safety alignment. Their greedy AdvTok search is competitive with GCG, AutoDAN and FFA and boosts them when combined, especially AutoDAN on Gemma2 and OLMo2. They also report increased safety-classifier bypass and prompt-injection success. They attribute the vulnerability to small-scale safety post-training and suggest building safety into pretraining.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses noncanonical-tokenization search and evaluates jailbreak attacks, rather than fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples or measuring aligned-versus-base KL by response position.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model and dataset. The paper reports that AdvTok's performance is more affected by the number of sampled neighbors than by the initial-tokenization seed, and reports prompt-length correlations that vary by model and attack method.

fits_no_version.finding: Compliance (StrongREJECT) rises with a tokenization's distance from canonical (Figure 5). AdvTok raises ASR and StrongREJECT over canonical prompts on all three models without changing the request text (Tables 1, 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety alignment is concentrated on the canonical tokenization of the prompt; noncanonical tokenizations of the same text partly evade it. This is input-side shallowness, distinct from first-response-token shallowness.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarially tokenized prompts are classified safe more often by LlamaGuard and ShieldGemma.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noncanonical tokenization increases bypass of dedicated safety classifiers. This is classifier detection, not chat-model compliance.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), 2025
record.problems: The paper states that attack evaluation uses 32 generated responses per attack and that prompt-injection evaluation uses an imperfect string-matching success criterion. The safety-classifier analysis reports high false-negative rates for ShieldGemma. Some reported metrics are evaluator-based; the text notes limitations of LLM-as-a-judge and uses StrongREJECT as an additional evaluator. Several results and ablations are presented in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Under the 60-row cap, retained canonical, GCG, AutoDAN, and AdvTok ASR rows, AdvTok StrongREJECT rows, and AdvTok safety-classifier bypass rows. Omitted Table 6 FFA and combined-method rows; Table 1 and Table 5 measurements for other methods; Table 2 methods other than canonical and AdvTok; and additional model-size, prompt-length, and hyperparameter ablations. These were not needed to cover the tested version and the main non-version-specific tokenization finding.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant response start; decoding changes; any test that bypass works by getting past the first response tokens. GCG and AutoDAN were run only as baselines, with 100 optimization steps.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Only an untested argument: post-training uses far less data than pretraining, so safety stays centred on canonical tokenization. No test of data or objective as a cause of first-token shallowness.

missing.what: StrongREJECT scores for GCG and AutoDAN versus canonical. Examples: Llama3 Masterkey GCG .258 and AutoDAN .146 vs canonical .272; OLMo2 Masterkey GCG .211 vs .231; Gemma2 AdvBench AutoDAN .429 vs .020.
Average Harmfulness Score for GCG and AutoDAN versus canonical across all models and datasets.
GCG and AutoDAN StrongREJECT across Llama3.2-1B, 3.2-3B and 3.1-8B. AutoDAN grows more effective with size (8B AdvBench .237 vs canonical .021); GCG barely moves at 8B (.029).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's labels put supports and limits_scope on the same V4 row set, which contradicts itself; this is replaced by one limits_scope label plus challenges for R09 and R26. GCG and AutoDAN are the study's comparison baselines run with reduced budgets (GCG 100 steps), which may understate suffix-attack strength. ASR counts only harmfulness score 5, judged by GPT-4o-mini, a strict threshold. Controls R01, R04, R07, R10, R13, R16, R19, R22 and R25 are canonical baselines and correctly carry cannot_determine. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning or post-fine-tuning refusal measurement.
No benign-data fine-tuning or resulting harmful-compliance measurement.
Tests GCG suffix attacks and AutoDAN prefix/suffix attacks, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; does not test a causal account based on getting past the first response tokens.
No weight or rank localization/ablation experiment.
Offers an argument about the relative scale of pretraining and post-training in tokenization space, but does not test whether data or objective causes first-token shallowness.
No training intended to deepen safety or test of whether deeper safety holds up.

relationships.condition: GCG and AutoDAN on Llama3-1B, Gemma2-2B and OLMo2-7B across AdvBench, Malicious and Masterkey, wherever ASR rises over canonical
relationships.reason: Suffix-type attacks raise extremely-harmful-output rates over canonical but mostly stay well below majority success. Examples: Llama3 GCG AdvBench 1.06% to 7.18%; OLMo2 GCG AdvBench 0.29% to 1.33%; the maximum is Gemma2 AutoDAN AdvBench at 49.3%. So suffixes only partly defeat refusal in this setting (R02, R03, R05, R06, R08, R11, R12, R14, R15, R17, R18, R20, R21, R23, R24, R27).
relationships.display_finding: Suffix-type attacks raised the rate of extremely harmful outputs over canonical tokenization, but mostly stayed low: for example 1.06% to 7.18% for Llama3 GCG on AdvBench and 0.29% to 1.33% for OLMo2 GCG. The highest rate was 49.3%, for Gemma2 AutoDAN on AdvBench.
